If you fell into a black hole, anyone watching would never actually see you fall in.
In 1916, a German soldier named Karl Schwarzschild solved Einstein's equations from the trenches of World War One. They predicted a place where gravity traps even light. He died just months later.
For decades it was just maths. Then in 2015, detectors in America felt a ripple from two black holes crashing together, one point three billion light years away.
In 2019, scientists took the first photo of one, six and a half billion times heavier than our Sun.
Get close to a small one, and gravity pulls your feet much harder than your head. You stretch like a noodle. Scientists call it spaghettification.
And they have watched it happen. In 2019, telescopes saw a star torn into a long stream as it fell into a black hole.
But a giant one is quieter. You would cross the edge without feeling a thing. No wall, no warning.
Because gravity bends time. To anyone far away, your clock slows down, your body turns red, and you seem to freeze at the edge.
You would be gone forever, while the outside world watched your fading image wait at the edge for eternity.
